The milk reform: who really pays the price? Every time they talk about agricultural reform, the story repeats itself: the agricultural lobby warns of a collapse, claims that the problem is not theirs at all, and promises that imports will not lower prices for the consumer. Now it's happening in the dairy farm. When you examine the matter without slogans but only facts, you see this: the dairy industry in Israel is one of the planned and centralized markets that exist: 🔹 The state determines how much milk will be produced 🔹 Who will be able to produce 🔹 And at what minimum price the dairies must buy? There is no competition, no entry of new players, and almost no imports - because of suffocating tariffs. And the result? High prices for the consumer, without direct connection to production efficiency. Even the "target price", which sounds neutral, is structured so that it is strongly influenced by small and expensive dairy farms - some of which do not participate in the cost survey at all. The proposed reform does not "eliminate agriculture", but changes the rules of the game: instead of closed quotas - protected liters at a lower price, opening the market, and creating an incentive for inefficient dairy farms to retire with compensation. And at the same time - a real possibility for importing and introducing new manufacturers. And those who claim that imports "do not pass on to the consumer" - should look at the fish market after the removal of tariffs in 2016 and 2022, frozen fish prices fell by 8.3%, while other food products jumped by more than 22%. The question now is: does the state manage a closed market for the benefit of an organized group, or does it open it to competition so that a basic product like milk is sold at a fair price? A role for selenium-dependent GPX1 in SARS-CoV-2 virulence "Among the proteins most impacted by selenium status is glutathione peroxidase 1 (GPX1), a cytosolic selenoenzyme with known antiviral properties. Viral infection increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in host cells, which, if not counterbalanced by antioxidant defense mechanisms, leads to oxidative stress. Excess oxidative stress, in turn, augments mutation of the viral genome, which can lead to the emergence of more virulent strains. GPX1 comprises a key defense against ROS, catalyzing the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide to water. In mice lacking the Gpx1 gene (Gpx1−/−), inoculation of a benign strain of coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) led to viral genome mutations, increased virulence, and myocarditis, none of which were observed in wild-type mice. Moreover, the Gpx1−/− model recapitulated the effect of a selenium-deficient diet in wild-type mice, promoting mutagenesis of the benign CVB3 strain into a virulent one. In addition, both selenium-deficient wild-type mice (6) and Gpx1−/− mice exhibit heightened inflammatory responses and more severe lung pathology in response to inoculation with influenza A, further indicating that GPX1 participates in molecular mechanisms protecting against viral infections of the respiratory tract. It is currently unknown whether SARS-CoV-2 is also modulated by GPX1 activity, but recent findings are highly suggestive."
